title: The Poetics of Space
author: Gaston Bachelard
coverAlt: Cover of The Poetics of Space by Gaston Bachelard (English edition)
body: Before any existential anguish, human beings are given a shelter: the house. And this shelter is not merely an architectural ensemble, but one of the fundamental conditions of our intimacy. The house we have lived in is, first of all, the space of our intimacy — the place that protects us and allows us to dream in peace. Without this shelter, a human being would be scattered before the storms of life.

To approach this understanding of the house, Bachelard proposes topoanalysis: a method of analysing the “happy spaces” that we inhabit emotionally and in which our intimacy is woven. His aim is to show that the places that become part of us cannot be understood through geometric rigour, but through direct experience, as lived spaces. A simple example can bring us closer to this kind of analysis: when we are small, the size of rooms and their layout in the house are not subject to objective measurement, but are distorted by the way we use and live in that space — a corner becomes huge if we spend whole hours playing there, a corridor seems endless if we are afraid to cross it at night. The childhood home, then, has no fixed geometry, but one shaped by feeling.

This distortion is not a perceptual error; it belongs to the nature of imagination as Bachelard understands it: a faculty of spontaneity, with an eminently productive vocation. In this sense, imagination does not simply reflect the world, but is active — it creates meaning. When I remember my childhood home, there is, for Bachelard, no point in describing it correctly in empirical terms. On the contrary, if I speak of this house from within my own imaginary, I will say something more precious and, importantly, just as real.

Reverie is what makes this experience of space possible. Unlike the night dream, reverie is the state of someone who dreams with their eyes open, what Bachelard calls a “cogito of reverie”. This state is awakened by contemplating ordinary phenomena or objects: a burning fire, a spiral staircase, a nest or a half-open door. Only when we enjoy the protection and intimacy of the house can we allow ourselves this suspension of reality, because reverie needs a safe environment in which to unfold.

From these moments of reverie comes topophilia, the deep attachment to spaces of refuge, such as the childhood home or one's own room. Beyond their obvious protective value, these beloved spaces are invested with imagined values — testimonies to the experience of whoever has lived in them.

In memory, the various dwellings of our lives intertwine, fixing moments of happiness and keeping the “treasures” of the past. The homes we have lived in are relived as present-day reveries, brought back to life in our present.
quote: “Before being ‘cast into the world’, as hasty metaphysics would have it, man is laid in the cradle of the house. And always, in our reveries, the house is a great cradle.”
quoteSource: — Gaston Bachelard, The Poetics of Space; translated from the Romanian edition (Poetica spațiului, trans. Irina Bădescu, Paralela 45, 2003, p. 38)

title: Real Utopias. The Utopian Body
author: Michel Foucault
coverAlt: Cover of the book Utopiile reale. Corpul utopic (Real Utopias. The Utopian Body) by Michel Foucault
body: The nineteenth century was obsessed with history — with development, with crisis, with the analysis of the past. We now live in an age of simultaneity, of juxtaposition, of the network — an age of space. And space is by no means neutral or empty: it carries with it its own history of how it has been thought.

Building on the cosmology of Aristotle, who divided the world into the sublunary and the supralunary, the Middle Ages kept a hierarchical organisation of space, with everything having its “natural” place somewhere on this scale. It was Galileo who broke the hierarchy: with him, space became infinite and open, with no absolute up or down. It might seem that we have escaped the old sacred oppositions. Foucault believes, however, that they have only been moved: private space is still opposed to public space, family space to social space, cultural space to useful space, the space of leisure to the space of work.
Utopia and heterotopia

Utopias are sites with no real place, which offer an image of society perfected or turned upside down, but imaginary in any case. Heterotopias, by contrast, are real: they are places that actually exist, but that contest reality.
The principles of heterotopia
1. Every human group creates its own heterotopias

So-called primitive societies have what Foucault calls crisis heterotopias: places reserved for those going through a moment of existential transition — adolescents, pregnant women, the elderly. Modernity replaced them with heterotopias of deviation — you no longer mark a stage of life, but a departure from the norm. The asylum, the psychiatric clinic, the prison, even the retirement home are, in this logic, so many spaces where society sets aside its own “deviant” members.
2. A heterotopia can change its function over time
Over the course of its history, a heterotopia can function in very different ways within the same society. The paradigmatic example Foucault offers is the cemetery.

“The cemetery is certainly an other place [un lieu autre] compared with ordinary cultural spaces, yet it is a space connected with all the sites of the city, or of society, or of the village, since every individual, every family has relatives in the cemetery. In Western culture, the cemetery has existed practically forever.” (p. 63)
Although the cemetery remains the same other kind of place, it is rethought over time: from a place at the heart of the community, next to the church, it becomes the marginal space of today.
3. A heterotopia juxtaposes incompatible spaces
A heterotopia can bring together, in a single real place, several spaces that normally could not coexist.

The illustrative example for this principle is the garden. The traditional Persian garden is conceived as a microcosm: divided into four parts, representing the four corners of the world, gathered around a sacred central point, like an umbilicus, “like the navel of the world at its centre”, where the ornamental pool with its fountain was placed. In a tiny space, such a garden condensed the whole universe.

The theatre can be understood in the same way, bringing onto one stage places and settings that are foreign to one another, as can the cinema, which projects a vast three-dimensional world onto a flat screen.
4. A heterotopia short-circuits the flow of time

Most of the time, heterotopias are marked by a break with “normal” time, and in this sense they can be called heterochronies. A heterotopia works to the full when people experience an absolute break with traditional time. Here too, the cemetery is the telling example: “the cemetery is truly a place that is heterotopic to the highest degree, since the cemetery begins with that strange heterochrony which, for an individual, is the loss of life, and with that quasi-eternity in which they never cease to dissolve and disappear.” (p. 66)

But heterotopias do not always mark an end: some accumulate time indefinitely, without an end point, like museums or libraries; others, on the contrary, are ephemeral, like the holiday village or the fair.
5. A heterotopia can only be entered through compulsion or ritual

You either have to enter a heterotopia, as with the barracks or the prison, or you must submit to rites and purifications. “Heterotopias always presuppose a system of opening and closing that both isolates them and makes them penetrable.” (p. 67)
6. A heterotopia has a function in relation to all the rest of space

The function of heterotopia unfolds between two opposite poles. At one end are heterotopias of illusion, places which, by their very existence, expose all the rest of the world as even more illusory. At the other end are heterotopias of compensation, places built as the perfect, ordered, meticulous reverse of a chaotic world.
quote: “I believe, in any case, that today's anxiety fundamentally concerns space, no doubt much more than time; time probably appears only as one of the possible games of distribution between the elements that are spread out in space.”
quoteSource: — Michel Foucault, Of Other Spaces; translated from the Romanian edition (Altfel de spații, in Utopiile reale. Corpul utopic, trans. Bogdan Ghiu, Tact, 2024, p. 59)

title: Life Between Buildings. Using Public Space
author: Jan Gehl
coverAlt: Cover of the book Viața între clădiri (Life Between Buildings. Using Public Space) by Jan Gehl
body: Architecture directly shapes the way we live, act and interact every day. For this reason, architects should be concerned not only with forms and functions, but also with people and the way they live — not only inside buildings, but outside them too. In Jan Gehl's view, the outside is at least as important as the inside for a community.

Public space is the in-between area among buildings, such as alleys, squares or courtyards. However, a space does not become “truly” public just because it exists or because it is not owned by an individual. It becomes public space only when people regularly fill it with their activities.

Jan Gehl divides activities in public space into three types: necessary (going to work or shopping), optional (taking a walk or reading on a bench) and social (children playing, greetings, conversations, the simple presence of others). A “healthy” public space would be one that gathers frequent and varied optional and social human activity.

Modern cities are often designed for the speed of cars, ignoring the human scale. At the natural pace of walking, people notice details, the faces of others, the texture of materials. A friendly urban space is built for the senses and the speed of the pedestrian, offering constant reasons to stop and look, as well as opportunities to connect with others.
quote: “If city planning and residential areas ensured optimal conditions for life in public spaces, many costly and far-fetched attempts to make buildings ‘interesting’ and complex through dramatic architectural effects could be avoided. That is because, in the long run, the life of public spaces is far more relevant and more interesting to contemplate than any architectural combination of coloured concrete and slanted planes.”
quoteSource: — Jan Gehl, Life Between Buildings; translated from the Romanian edition (Viața între clădiri, trans. Silvia Gugu, Igloo Media, 2024, p. 22)

title: Socrates' Ancestor
author: Indra Kagis McEwen
coverAlt: Cover of the book Străbunul lui Socrate (Socrates' Ancestor) by Indra Kagis McEwen
body: What do we actually know about the origins of architecture? Not just about styles or building techniques, but about the original gesture through which people began to think of space as something that can be produced, ordered, inhabited with intention? This is the question Indra Kagis McEwen asks in Socrates' Ancestor, following in the footsteps of Heidegger's thought. Her position may seem surprising: architecture does not begin with matter, nor with the plan, but with the gesture of the body in space.

McEwen is not interested in buildings as objects, but in architecture as a way of being in the world. To this end, she goes back to the roots of archaic Greek thought, where philosophy, cosmology, ritual and building were not yet separate fields, but expressions of the same impulse: to make the world legible, to order it and to make it habitable. Making order (kosmos) out of chaos is the beginning of every act of building. This order can be found in the weaving of a garment, in the coordinated movement of bodies in a shared space, in finding one's way across the vast open space of the sea or the sky, in tracing a boundary that separates the sacred from the profane. All of these are, from her perspective, forms of architecture before Architecture — ways of making the world legible before building in the strict sense.

One of the book's most fertile arguments is that space does not exist independently of the body that produces it. The argument is illustrated through choros — the Homeric term that designates both the dance and the dancing place. The place of the choros does not exist before the dance and disappears once it has ended. Space is not a neutral container in which things happen — it is an effect, a consequence of human gesture.

Another thread is the word ptera, “wings”. In archaic Greek, the same word designates the wings of a bird, the oars of a boat and the colonnade surrounding a temple. Well-fitted oars are, for the Greeks, the expression of eurythmia: the perfect fit of a form to its surrounding element. The term derives from eu, “well”, and rhythmos, understood not as mere rhythm but as a pattern isolated within a continuous movement, able to convey the whole nature of that movement. This is exactly what the builders of the first peripteral temples were after. When they raised colonnades, they were in fact raising looms — the post-and-beam structure most familiar to the Greek world, present in every household. And when the temple becomes peripteral, it acquires ptera, wings. Naos and naus — the sanctuary and the ship — were not just related words, but overlapping images: the peripteral temple was a ship rooted in its sacred place, yet conceived to fly.

The argument reaches its peak in the Parthenon: its refinements are not mere optical corrections, but the expression of a tension between movement and fixity — like a bow drawn taut, about to release an arrow, like sails swollen by the wind. The Parthenon seems to take wing. Architecture is not “rooted”: it was conceived from the very beginning as flight and navigation.

Behind this argument stands the figure of Daedalus. The myth of his son, Icarus, comes in two versions, both highlighting the limits of mastering space: in the familiar one, Icarus flies too close to the sun and falls; in the other, he drowns near Samos because he is not a good navigator like his father. The same failure shows itself in two different elements. Flying and navigating are practices of the limit, of finding the right bearing in a space that can destroy you — chaos. Daedalus masters both.

His name is also linked to the word daidalon, the Homeric term for something made with supreme skill, tightly woven like the joints of a ship, endowed with a shimmering surface — an epiphaneia, an “appearance”, as McEwen calls it. A daidalon is not a mere object: it has the capacity to appear, to make visible what would otherwise remain hidden. And techné, the craft of Daedalus, does not mean technical skill in the modern sense. Its roots, tiktein (“to give birth”) and tektein (“to build”), originally mean the same thing: to let something appear. Daedalus is the first architect not because of the buildings he raised, but because he embodies the fact that building is, at heart, a gesture of making order visible in the world. “The craftsman lets the kosmos appear through the artefact.”

title: Common Space. The City as Commons
author: Stavros Stavrides
coverAlt: Cover of the book Spațiul comun. Orașul ca bun comun (Common Space. The City as Commons) by Stavros Stavrides
body: Contemporary cities seem increasingly organised around economic priorities and the logic of profit. The way spaces are built, divided and used seems to follow a web of economic relations whose ultimate aim is to maximise profit. In this context, Stavros Stavrides sets out to study the forms of resistance and the creative alternatives that emerge within cities, defying this logic.

In many parts of the world, when people oppose unjust policies, corrupt governments or exploitation, they begin to organise their shared life themselves. To explain this phenomenon, Stavrides proposes a distinction between three types of space:

• Private space is an eminently closed space, defined by a relationship of ownership and with very clear rules of access for outsiders: one's own apartment, a café, a mall, etc.
  • Public space is owned and managed by the public administration: streets, squares, small plazas, the steps of public institutions, etc. The rules for using these spaces are set by an authority, not by those who use them.
  • Common space, the one Stavrides is interested in, works differently: its rules are negotiated within the community that uses it.

Common space has no exact position on the map of a city or a village; it is a mobile “structure”, so to speak. It shelters a “porous world”, whose exact counterpoint is the world of urban enclaves, of sharply bounded neighbourhoods (enclaves of poverty or of privilege), or of other urban spaces whose function is defined from the top down and which, by implication, impose a certain conduct, usually acting as catalysts of social reproduction.

Common space is a space of resistance to these “pre-existing taxonomies” that define roles and identities. It is close to heterotopia in that it blurs traditional divisions and brings together what is usually kept apart. It is a potential “meeting ground” between equals, beyond each person's socio-economic status, beyond ideologies, and so on, with all their differences — which is why a common space is not one where belonging to a group or to a well-defined identity takes priority.

Since it is not a good or a clearly bounded place, a territory, common space does not exist as such, but emerges every time certain ways of being together come into play. In other words, common space is more of a process and belongs to the category of activity. Stavrides calls this practice commoning. In relation to imposed definitions and taxonomies, common space is a threshold space, between worlds, a passage that connects different identities and personal narratives.

Although it originally emerges through the practice of being in common, common space can settle in a place and give rise to an autonomous, self-managed form of living together. One example Stavrides discusses is Navarinou Park, in the Exarcheia neighbourhood of Athens, where local residents reclaimed a car park to turn it into a jointly run park.

Settling common space in a bounded place brings the risk of it becoming an enclave. To remain truly common, such spaces must keep four qualities: (1) they refuse to let hierarchical relations take hold; (2) they constantly practise translation and openness towards “newcomers”; (3) they invent mechanisms to prevent the accumulation of power (rotating tasks, distributing decision-making, decentralisation, etc.); (4) they are, most likely, spaces where giving is practised — defined by Stavrides as offering more than what you may receive in return.
Described in this way, common spaces are not mere meeting places, but an alternative and a form of resistance to the state and to profit-driven urban organisation.
quote: “From the perspective of reclaiming the city, common spaces are nodes through which the metropolis once again becomes the place of politics, if by ‘politics’ we can describe an open process through which the dominant forms of living together are questioned and possibly transformed.”
quoteSource: — Stavros Stavrides, Common Space. The City as Commons; translated from the Romanian edition (Spațiul comun. Orașul ca bun comun, trans. Deniz Otay and Ilinca Pop, Vellant, 2023, p. 72)
